# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Unwrap](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)- Err
- Wrapper around `TryRng``Rng`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html)
- The error type for errors that can never happen.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- Trait for infallible random number generators
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)- Deprecated
- DEPRECATED: stub trait to print a deprecation warning and aid discovering that `Rng`
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `TryRng`
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)
- Base trait for random number generators and random data sources
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRngCore.html)- Core - Deprecated
- DEPRECATED: stub trait to print a deprecation warning and aid discovering that `TryRng`

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

---

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

---

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distr](https://docs.rs/distr/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [RngReader](https://docs.rs/struct.RngReader.html)- `std`
- Adapter to support `std::io::Read``TryRng`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Support filling a slice with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- Trait for infallible random number generators
- [RngExt](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html)
- User-level interface for RNGs
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `TryRng`
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)
- Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill](https://docs.rs/fn.fill.html)- `thread_rng`
- Fill any type implementing `Fill`
- [make_](https://docs.rs/fn.make_rng.html)- rng - `sys_rng`
- Construct and seed an RNG
- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_bool.html)- bool - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability `p`of being true.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_iter.html)- iter - `thread_rng`
- Return an iterator over `random()`
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_range.html)- range - `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value in the given range using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_ratio.html)- ratio - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator`of being true.
- [rng](https://docs.rs/fn.rng.html)- `thread_rng`
- Access a fast, pre-initialized generator

# rand_core 0.10.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1

# rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

## License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

---

[37](https://docs.rs#37)/// sequences. In particular, [`rand::RngExt`] is an extension trait over `Rng`

[90](https://docs.rs#90)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs
[92](https://docs.rs#92)///
[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// This is a convenient trait alias for <code>[TryCryptoRng]<Error = [Infallible]></code>.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// It is equivalent to the trait sum <code>[Rng] + [TryCryptoRng]</code>.
[95](https://docs.rs#95)pub trait [CryptoRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/trait.CryptoRng.html): [Rng](https://docs.rs#49-63) + [TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs#249)<Error = [Infallible](https://docs.rs/rand_core/enum.Infallible.html)> {}
[96](https://docs.rs#96)
[97](https://docs.rs#97)impl<R> [CryptoRng](https://docs.rs#95) for R where R: [TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs#249)<Error = [Infallible](https://docs.rs/rand_core/enum.Infallible.html)> + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {}
[98](https://docs.rs#98)
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// Base trait for random number generators and random data sources
[100](https://docs.rs#100)///
[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// (`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// of [`try_fill_bytes`](Self::try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// to avoid storing a partially used word or block.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// # Requirements
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// ### Quality and length
[111](https://docs.rs#111)///
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// uniform-ranged distribution).
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// but is a requirement of [`TryCryptoRng`].
[125](https://docs.rs#125)///
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality][0].
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// [0]: https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality
[135](https://docs.rs#135)///
[136](https://docs.rs#136)/// ### Reproducibility
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// Algorithmic generators implementing [`SeedableRng`] should normally have
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// *portable, reproducible* output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes).
[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// See also [The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility][1].
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// [1]: https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// # Usage
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// Often, usage of the infallible trait [`Rng`] or its extension trait
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// [`rand::RngExt`] is preferred to direct usage of `TryRng`.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with <code>type Error = [Infallible][]</code>)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// already implement [`Rng`]; in other cases [`UnwrapErr`] may be used to obtain
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// an implementation of [`Rng`].
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// # Implementing `TryRng`
[156](https://docs.rs#156)///
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [`Infallible`]; in this case
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// trait `Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// error.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)///
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)/// Module [`crate::utils`] provides utilities to help implement other methods.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// Byte sources may implement [`try_fill_bytes`](Self::try_fill_bytes)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// natively.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)/// Module [`crate::utils`] provides utilities to help implement other methods.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)///
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// should make use of the [`crate::block`] module.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// With regards to other traits:
[173](https://docs.rs#173)///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)/// - **Do not** implement [`Default`] for seedable pseudorandom generators,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)///   though the trait may be implemented for stateless interfaces and
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///   auto-seeding generators.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// - **Do** implement [`SeedableRng`] for seedable pseudorandom generators. See
[178](https://docs.rs#178)///   [Reproducibility](#reproducibility) above.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// - Implement [`Clone`] for non-cryptographic PRNGs but consider not doing so
[180](https://docs.rs#180)///   for cryptographic generators to avoid the risk of key-stream duplication.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// - **Do not** implement [`Copy`] since accidental copies may cause repeated
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///   values.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)/// - Implement [`Debug`](core::fmt::Debug), except that cryptographic PRNGs
[184](https://docs.rs#184)///   should use a custom implementation which avoids leaking internal state (or
[185](https://docs.rs#185)///   the subset of this derived from the key).
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// - [`Eq`] and [`PartialEq`] could be implemented, but are probably not useful.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// [`rand::RngExt`]: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html
[189](https://docs.rs#189)pub trait [TryRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/trait.TryRng.html) {

[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// A marker trait over [`TryRng`] for securely unpredictable RNGs
[226](https://docs.rs#226)///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// This marker trait indicates that the implementing generator is intended,
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// when correctly seeded and protected from side-channel attacks such as a
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// leaking of state, to be a cryptographically secure generator. This trait is
[230](https://docs.rs#230)/// provided as a tool to aid review of cryptographic code, but does not by
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// itself guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)///
[233](https://docs.rs#233)/// Formally, a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)/// should satisfy an additional property over other generators: assuming that
[235](https://docs.rs#235)/// the generator has been appropriately seeded and has unknown state, then
[236](https://docs.rs#236)/// given the first *k* bits of an algorithm's output
[237](https://docs.rs#237)/// sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)///
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// An optional property of CSPRNGs is backtracking resistance: if the CSPRNG's
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// state is revealed, it will not be computationally-feasible to reconstruct
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// prior output values. This property is not required by `CryptoRng`.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)///
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// Implementors of `TryCryptoRng` should only implement [`Default`] if a
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// default-constructed instance is itself a secure generator, for example
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// [`getrandom::SysRng`] which is a stateless interface.
[247](https://docs.rs#247)///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// [`getrandom::SysRng`]: https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/struct.SysRng.html
[249](https://docs.rs#249)pub trait [TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/trait.TryCryptoRng.html): [TryRng](https://docs.rs#189-201) {}

A random (block) generator

The output type.

For use with `rand_core::block``[u32; _]` or `[u64; _]`.

Generate a new block of `output`.

This must fill `output` with random data.

Destruct the output buffer

# BlockRng in rand_core::block - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/rand_core/block/struct.BlockRng.html

`pub struct BlockRng<G: `[Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html)> {
    pub core: G,
    /* private fields */
}## Expand description

RNG functionality for a block `Generator`

This type encompasses a `Generator`[ core](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html#structfield.core) and a buffer.
It provides optimized implementations of methods required by an

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`All values are consumed in-order of generation. No whole words (e.g. `u32`
or `u64`) are discarded, though where a word is partially used (e.g. for a
byte-fill whose length is not a multiple of the word size) the rest of the
word is discarded.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.core)

`core: G`The *core* part of the RNG, implementing the `generate` function.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#195-204)#### pub fn [reset_and_skip](https://docs.rs#method.reset_and_skip)(&mut self, n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#195-204)

#### pub fn [reset_and_skip](https://docs.rs#method.reset_and_skip)(&mut self, n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html))

Re-generate buffer contents, skipping the first `n` words

Existing buffer contents are discarded. A new set of results is
generated (either immediately or when next required). The first `n`
words are skipped (this may be used to set a specific word position).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This method will panic if `n >= N` where `N` is the buffer size (in
words).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#211-214)#### pub fn [word_offset](https://docs.rs#method.word_offset)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#211-214)

#### pub fn [word_offset](https://docs.rs#method.word_offset)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)

Get the number of words consumed since the start of the block

The result is in the range `0..N` where `N` is the buffer size (in
words).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#225-228)#### pub fn [remaining_results](https://docs.rs#method.remaining_results)(&self) -> &[[W]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.slice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#225-228)

#### pub fn [remaining_results](https://docs.rs#method.remaining_results)(&self) -> &[[W]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.slice.html)

Access the unused part of the results buffer

The length of the returned slice is guaranteed to be less than the
length of `<Self as Generator>::Output` (i.e. less than `N` where
`Output = [W; N]`).

This is a low-level interface intended for serialization. Results are not marked as consumed.

# UnwrapErr in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/rand_core/struct.UnwrapErr.html

`pub struct UnwrapErr<R: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)>(pub R);## Expand description

Wrapper around [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) implementation which implements

[by panicking on potential errors.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
fn with_try_rng<R: TryRng>(mut rng: R) {
    // rng does not impl Rng:
    let _ = rng.try_next_u32(); // okay
    // let _ = rng.next_u32(); // error
    // An adapter borrowing rng:
    let _ = UnwrapErr(&mut rng).next_u32();
    // An adapter moving rng:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
fn call_with_unsized_try_rng<R: TryRng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) {
    // R is unsized, thus we must use &mut R:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
```
## Tuple Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.0)

`0: R`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reborrow with a new lifetime

Rust allows references like `&T` or `&mut T` to be “reborrowed” through
coercion: essentially, the pointer is copied under a new, shorter, lifetime.
Until rfcs#1403 lands, reborrows on user types require a method call.

# TryRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/rand_core/trait.TryRng.html

```
pub trait TryRng {
    type
```
[Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error): [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html);
    // Required methods
    fn [try_next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u32)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u64)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
(`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
of [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
to avoid storing a partially used word or block.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#quality-and-length)Quality and length

Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).

Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a uniform-ranged distribution).

Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
but is a requirement of [ TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html).

In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.

For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality).

[§](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)Reproducibility

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes). See also

[The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Often, usage of the infallible trait [ Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) or its extension trait

[is preferred to direct usage of](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``TryRng`.
Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with `type Error = `[Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html))
already implement [; in other cases](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[may be used to obtain an implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)

`UnwrapErr`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-tryrng)Implementing `TryRng`

Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [ Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html); in this case
trait

`Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
error.Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
Module [ crate::utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html) provides utilities to help implement other methods.

Byte sources may implement [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)
natively.
Module

[provides utilities to help implement other methods.](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)

`crate::utils`Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
should make use of the [ crate::block](https://docs.rs/block/index.html) module.

With regards to other traits:

- **Do not**implement- `Default`
- **Do**implement- `SeedableRng`- [Reproducibility](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)above.
- Implement `Clone`
- **Do not**implement- `Copy`
- Implement `Debug`

# Infallible in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/rand_core/enum.Infallible.html

`pub enum Infallible {}`## Expand description

The error type for errors that can never happen.

Since this enum has no variant, a value of this type can never actually exist.
This can be useful for generic APIs that use [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html) and parameterize the error type,
to indicate that the result is always

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)

`Ok`For example, the [ TryFrom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html) trait (conversion that returns a

[) has a blanket implementation for all types where a reverse](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[implementation exists.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T, U> TryFrom<U> for T where U: Into<T> {
    type Error = Infallible;
    fn try_from(value: U) -> Result<Self, Infallible> {
        Ok(U::into(value))  // Never returns `Err`
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#future-compatibility)Future compatibility

This enum has the same role as [the  ! “never” type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.never.html),
which is unstable in this version of Rust.
When

`!` is stabilized, we plan to make `Infallible` a type alias to it:… and eventually deprecate `Infallible`.

However there is one case where `!` syntax can be used
before `!` is stabilized as a full-fledged type: in the position of a function’s return type.
Specifically, it is possible to have implementations for two different function pointer types:

```
trait MyTrait {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> ! {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> std::convert::Infallible {}
```
With `Infallible` being an enum, this code is valid.
However when `Infallible` becomes an alias for the never type,
the two `impl`s will start to overlap
and therefore will be disallowed by the language’s trait coherence rules.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# SeedableRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html

`pub trait SeedableRng: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    type [Seed](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Seed): [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]> + [AsMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsMut.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]>;
    // Required method
    fn [from_seed](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_seed)(seed: Self::[Seed](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#associatedtype.Seed)) -> Self;
    // Provided methods
    fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self { ... }
[from_rng](https://docs.rs#method.from_rng)<R: [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(rng: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)) -> Self { ... }
[try_from_rng](https://docs.rs#method.try_from_rng)<R: [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(rng: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, R::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)> { ... }
[fork](https://docs.rs#method.fork)(&mut self) -> Self
       where Self: [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) { ... }
[try_fork](https://docs.rs#method.try_fork)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where Self: [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all pseudo-random number generators (PRNGs, or algorithmic generators).

A generator implementing `SeedableRng` will usually be deterministic, but
beware that portability and reproducibility of results **is not implied**.
Refer to documentation of the generator, noting that generators named after
a specific algorithm are usually tested for reproducibility against a
reference vector, while `SmallRng` and `StdRng` specifically opt out of
reproducibility guarantees.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

Seed type, which is restricted to types mutably-dereferenceable as `u8`
arrays (we recommend `[u8; N]` for some `N`).

It is recommended to seed PRNGs with a seed of at least circa 100 bits,
which means an array of `[u8; 12]` or greater to avoid picking RNGs with
partially overlapping periods.

For cryptographic RNG’s a seed of 256 bits is recommended, `[u8; 32]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng-for-rngs-with-large-seeds)Implementing `SeedableRng` for RNGs with large seeds

Note that [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) is not implemented for large arrays

`[u8; N]` with
`N` > 32. To be able to implement the traits required by `SeedableRng`
for RNGs with such large seeds, the newtype pattern can be used:```
use rand_core::SeedableRng;
const N: usize = 64;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct MyRngSeed(pub [u8; N]);
pub struct MyRng(MyRngSeed);
impl Default for MyRngSeed {
    fn default() -> MyRngSeed {
        MyRngSeed([0; N])
    }
}
impl AsRef<[u8]> for MyRngSeed {
    fn as_ref(&self) -> &[u8] {
        &self.0
    }
}
impl AsMut<[u8]> for MyRngSeed {
    fn as_mut(&mut self) -> &mut [u8] {
        &mut self.0
    }
}
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = MyRngSeed;
    fn from_seed(seed: MyRngSeed) -> MyRng {
        MyRng(seed)
    }
}
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Create a new PRNG using the given seed.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that bits in the seed are
well distributed. That means usually that the number of one and zero
bits are roughly equal, and values like 0, 1 and (size - 1) are unlikely.
Note that many non-cryptographic PRNGs will show poor quality output
if this is not adhered to. If you wish to seed from simple numbers, use
`seed_from_u64` instead.

All PRNG implementations should be reproducible unless otherwise noted:
given a fixed `seed`, the same sequence of output should be produced
on all runs, library versions and architectures (e.g. check endianness).
Any “value-breaking” changes to the generator should require bumping at
least the minor version and documentation of the change.

It is not required that this function yield the same state as a reference implementation of the PRNG given equivalent seed; if necessary another constructor replicating behaviour from a reference implementation can be added.

PRNG implementations should make sure `from_seed` never panics. In the
case that some special values (like an all zero seed) are not viable
seeds it is preferable to map these to alternative constant value(s),
for example `0xBAD5EEDu32` or `0x0DDB1A5E5BAD5EEDu64` (“odd biases? bad
seed”). This is assuming only a small number of values must be rejected.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/seedable_rng.rs.html#109-121)#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/seedable_rng.rs.html#109-121)

#### fn [seed_from_u64](https://docs.rs#method.seed_from_u64)(state: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html)) -> Self

Create a new PRNG using a `u64` seed.

This is a convenience-wrapper around `from_seed` to allow construction
of any `SeedableRng` from a simple `u64` value. It is designed such that
low Hamming Weight numbers like 0 and 1 can be used and should still
result in good, independent seeds to the PRNG which is returned.

This **is not suitable for cryptography**, as should be clear given that
the input size is only 64 bits.

Implementations for PRNGs *may* provide their own implementations of
this function, but the default implementation should be good enough for
all purposes. *Changing* the implementation of this function should be
considered a value-breaking change.

Create a new PRNG seeded from an infallible `Rng`.

This may be useful when needing to rapidly seed many PRNGs from a master PRNG, and to allow forking of PRNGs. It may be considered deterministic.

The master PRNG should be at least as high quality as the child PRNGs.
When seeding non-cryptographic child PRNGs, we recommend using a
different algorithm for the master PRNG (ideally a CSPRNG) to avoid
correlations between the child PRNGs. If this is not possible (e.g.
forking using small non-crypto PRNGs) ensure that your PRNG has a good
mixing function on the output or consider use of a hash function with
`from_seed`.

Note that seeding `XorShiftRng` from another `XorShiftRng` provides an
extreme example of what can go wrong: the new PRNG will be a clone
of the parent.

PRNG implementations are allowed to assume that a good RNG is provided
for seeding, and that it is cryptographically secure when appropriate.
As of `rand` 0.7 / `rand_core` 0.5, implementations overriding this
method should ensure the implementation satisfies reproducibility
(in prior versions this was not required).

Fork this PRNG

This creates a new PRNG from the current one by initializing a new one and seeding it from the current one.

This is useful when initializing a PRNG for a thread

Fork this PRNG

This creates a new PRNG from the current one by initializing a new one and seeding it from the current one.

This is useful when initializing a PRNG for a thread.

This is the failable equivalent to `SeedableRng::fork`

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# TryCryptoRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/rand_core/trait.TryCryptoRng.html

`pub trait TryCryptoRng: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) { }## Expand description

A marker trait over [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) for securely unpredictable RNGs

This marker trait indicates that the implementing generator is intended, when correctly seeded and protected from side-channel attacks such as a leaking of state, to be a cryptographically secure generator. This trait is provided as a tool to aid review of cryptographic code, but does not by itself guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications.

Formally, a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
should satisfy an additional property over other generators: assuming that
the generator has been appropriately seeded and has unknown state, then
given the first *k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

An optional property of CSPRNGs is backtracking resistance: if the CSPRNG’s
state is revealed, it will not be computationally-feasible to reconstruct
prior output values. This property is not required by `CryptoRng`.

Implementors of `TryCryptoRng` should only implement [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) if a
default-constructed instance is itself a secure generator, for example

[which is a stateless interface.](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/struct.SysRng.html)

`getrandom::SysRng`

---

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

- DEPRECATED: stub trait to print a deprecation warning and aid discovering that `Rng`

# rand_core - Rust

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

# rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

# rand_core 0.10.0-rc-2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.0-rc-2

# rand_core

Core traits and error types of the [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) library, plus tools for implementing
RNGs.

This crate is intended for use when implementing the core trait, `RngCore`; it
defines the core traits to be implemented as well as several small functions to
aid in their implementation and types required for error handling.

The main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate re-exports most items defined in this crate, along with
tools to convert the integer samples generated by `RngCore` to many different
applications (including sampling from restricted ranges, conversion to floating
point, list permutations and secure initialisation of RNGs). Most users should
prefer to use the main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate.

Links:

## Functionality

The `rand_core` crate provides:

- base random number generator traits
- error-reporting types
- functionality to aid implementation of RNGs

The traits and error types are also available via `rand`.

## Versions

The current version is:

```
 = "0.9.3"
```
# License

`rand_core` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# rand_core 0.9.0-alpha.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.9.0-alpha.1

# rand_core

Core traits and error types of the [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) library, plus tools for implementing
RNGs.

This crate is intended for use when implementing the core trait, `RngCore`; it
defines the core traits to be implemented as well as several small functions to
aid in their implementation and types required for error handling.

The main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate re-exports most items defined in this crate, along with
tools to convert the integer samples generated by `RngCore` to many different
applications (including sampling from restricted ranges, conversion to floating
point, list permutations and secure initialisation of RNGs). Most users should
prefer to use the main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate.

Links:

## Functionality

The `rand_core` crate provides:

- base random number generator traits
- error-reporting types
- functionality to aid implementation of RNGs

The traits and error types are also available via `rand`.

## Versions

The current version is:

```
rand_core = "0.6.4"
```
Rand libs have inter-dependencies and make use of the
[semver trick](https://github.com/dtolnay/semver-trick/) in order to make traits
compatible across crate versions. (This is especially important for `RngCore`
and `SeedableRng`.) A few crate releases are thus compatibility shims,
depending on the *next* lib version (e.g. `rand_core` versions `0.2.2` and
`0.3.1`). This means, for example, that `rand_core_0_4_0::SeedableRng` and
`rand_core_0_3_0::SeedableRng` are distinct, incompatible traits, which can
cause build errors. Usually, running `cargo update` is enough to fix any issues.

## Crate Features

`rand_core` supports `no_std` and `alloc`-only configurations, as well as full
`std` functionality. The differences between `no_std` and full `std` are small,
comprising `RngCore` support for `Box<R>` types where `R: RngCore`,
`std::io::Read` support for types supporting `RngCore`, and
extensions to the `Error` type's functionality.

The `std` feature is *not enabled by default*. This is primarily to avoid build
problems where one crate implicitly requires `rand_core` with `std` support and
another crate requires `rand` *without* `std` support. However, the `rand` crate
continues to enable `std` support by default, both for itself and `rand_core`.

The `serde1` feature can be used to derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize` for RNG
implementations that use the `BlockRng` or `BlockRng64` wrappers.

# License

`rand_core` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

---

problems where one crate implicitly requires `rand_core` with `std` support and
another crate requires `rand` *without* `std` support. However, the `rand` crate
continues to enable `std` support by default, both for itself and `rand_core`.

The `serde1` feature can be used to derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize` for RNG
implementations that use the `BlockRng` or `BlockRng64` wrappers.

# License

`rand_core` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

# rand_core 0.6.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.6.4

# rand_core

Core traits and error types of the [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) library, plus tools for implementing
RNGs.

This crate is intended for use when implementing the core trait, `RngCore`; it
defines the core traits to be implemented as well as several small functions to
aid in their implementation and types required for error handling.

The main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate re-exports most items defined in this crate, along with
tools to convert the integer samples generated by `RngCore` to many different
applications (including sampling from restricted ranges, conversion to floating
point, list permutations and secure initialisation of RNGs). Most users should
prefer to use the main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate.

Links:

## Functionality

The `rand_core` crate provides:

- base random number generator traits
- error-reporting types
- functionality to aid implementation of RNGs

The traits and error types are also available via `rand`.

## Versions

The current version is:

```
rand_core = "0.6.0"
```
Rand libs have inter-dependencies and make use of the
[semver trick](https://github.com/dtolnay/semver-trick/) in order to make traits
compatible across crate versions. (This is especially important for `RngCore`
and `SeedableRng`.) A few crate releases are thus compatibility shims,
depending on the *next* lib version (e.g. `rand_core` versions `0.2.2` and
`0.3.1`). This means, for example, that `rand_core_0_4_0::SeedableRng` and
`rand_core_0_3_0::SeedableRng` are distinct, incompatible traits, which can
cause build errors. Usually, running `cargo update` is enough to fix any issues.

## Crate Features

`rand_core` supports `no_std` and `alloc`-only configurations, as well as full
`std` functionality. The differences between `no_std` and full `std` are small,
comprising `RngCore` support for `Box<R>` types where `R: RngCore`,
`std::io::Read` support for types supporting `RngCore`, and
extensions to the `Error` type's functionality.

The `std` feature is *not enabled by default*. This is primarily to avoid build
problems where one crate implicitly requires `rand_core` with `std` support and
another crate requires `rand` *without* `std` support. However, the `rand` crate
continues to enable `std` support by default, both for itself and `rand_core`.

The `serde1` feature can be used to derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize` for RNG
implementations that use the `BlockRng` or `BlockRng64` wrappers.

# License

`rand_core` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

---

implementations that use the `BlockRng` or `BlockRng64` wrappers.

# rand_core 0.3.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.3.0

# rand_core

Core traits and error types of the [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) library, plus tools for implementing
RNGs.

This crate is intended for use when implementing the core trait, `RngCore`; it
defines the core traits to be implemented as well as several small functions to
aid in their implementation and types required for error handling.

The main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate re-exports most items defined in this crate, along with
tools to convert the integer samples generated by `RngCore` to many different
applications (including sampling from restricted ranges, conversion to floating
point, list permutations and secure initialisation of RNGs). Most users should
prefer to use the main [rand](https://crates.io/crates/rand) crate.

Documentation:
[master branch](https://rust-random.github.io/rand/rand_core/index.html),
[by release](https://docs.rs/rand_core)

## Functionality

The `rand_core` crate provides:

- base random number generator traits
- error-reporting types
- functionality to aid implementation of RNGs

The traits and error types are also available via `rand`.

## Crate Features

`rand_core` supports `no_std` and `alloc`-only configurations, as well as full
`std` functionality. The differences between `no_std` and full `std` are small,
comprising `RngCore` support for `Box<R>` types where `R: RngCore`, as well as
extensions to the `Error` type's functionality.

Due to [rust-lang/cargo#1596](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/1596),
`rand_core` is built without `std` support by default. Since features are
unioned across the whole dependency tree, any crate using `rand` with its
default features will also enable `std` support in `rand_core`.

The `serde1` feature can be used to derive `Serialize` and `Deserialize` for RNG
implementations that use the `BlockRng` or `BlockRng64` wrappers.

# License

`rand_core` is distributed under the terms of both the MIT license and the
Apache License (Version 2.0).

See [LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE) and [LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT), and
[COPYRIGHT](https://docs.rs/COPYRIGHT) for details.

---

# rand_core 0.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.0.1

# rand

Core functionality for the [rand](https://docs.rs/) library.

This crate contains the core trait, `Rng`, and some extension traits. This
should be sufficient for libraries publishing an RNG type, but most users should
prefer to use the [rand](https://docs.rs/) crate.

## Status

This crate is experimental, provided as part of the [rand crate refactor](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2106). Users
should be wary of depending on this crate at this time; breaking changes should
be expected and contents will conflict with those of the current published
version of rand (0.3.x).

# License

`rand` is primarily distributed under the terms of both the MIT
license and the Apache License (Version 2.0), with portions covered by various
BSD-like licenses.

See LICENSE-APACHE, and LICENSE-MIT for details.

---

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Unwrap](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)- Err
- Wrapper around `TryRng``Rng`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html)
- The error type for errors that can never happen.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- Trait for infallible random number generators
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)- Deprecated
- DEPRECATED: stub trait to print a deprecation warning and aid discovering that `Rng`
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `TryRng`
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)
- Base trait for random number generators and random data sources
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRngCore.html)- Core - Deprecated
- DEPRECATED: stub trait to print a deprecation warning and aid discovering that `TryRng`

# rand_core::block - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/index.html

## Expand description

The [ Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html) trait and

`BlockRng`Trait [ Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html) may be implemented by block-generators; that is PRNGs
whose output is a

*block*of words, such as

`[u32; 16]`.The struct [ BlockRng](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html) wraps such a

[together with an output buffer and implements several methods (e.g.](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html)

`Generator`[) to assist in the implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html#method.next_word)

`BlockRng::next_word`[. Note that (unlike in earlier versions of](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)

`TryRng``rand_core`) [itself does not implement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html)

`BlockRng`[since in practice we found it was always beneficial to use a wrapper type over](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)

`TryRng`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html)

`BlockRng`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use core::convert::Infallible;
use rand_core::{Rng, SeedableRng, TryRng};
use rand_core::block::{Generator, BlockRng};
struct MyRngCore {
    // Generator state ...
}
impl Generator for MyRngCore {
    type Output = [u32; 8];
    fn generate(&mut self, output: &mut Self::Output) {
        // Write a new block to output...
    }
}
// Our RNG is a wrapper over BlockRng
pub struct MyRng(BlockRng<MyRngCore>);
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = [u8; 32];
    fn from_seed(seed: Self::Seed) -> Self {
        let core = MyRngCore {
            // ...
        };
        MyRng(BlockRng::new(core))
    }
}
impl TryRng for MyRng {
    type Error = Infallible;
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.next_word())
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.next_u64_from_u32())
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, bytes: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.fill_bytes(bytes))
    }
}
// And if applicable: impl TryCryptoRng for MyRng {}
let mut rng = MyRng::seed_from_u64(0);
println!("First value: {}", rng.next_u32());
```

# BlockRng in rand_core::block - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/struct.BlockRng.html

`pub struct BlockRng<G: `[Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html)> {
    pub core: G,
    /* private fields */
}## Expand description

RNG functionality for a block `Generator`

This type encompasses a `Generator`[ core](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html#structfield.core) and a buffer.
It provides optimized implementations of methods required by an

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`All values are consumed in-order of generation. No whole words (e.g. `u32`
or `u64`) are discarded, though where a word is partially used (e.g. for a
byte-fill whose length is not a multiple of the word size) the rest of the
word is discarded.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.core)

`core: G`The *core* part of the RNG, implementing the `generate` function.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#195-204)

#### pub fn [reset_and_skip](https://docs.rs#method.reset_and_skip)(&mut self, n: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html))

Re-generate buffer contents, skipping the first `n` words

Existing buffer contents are discarded. A new set of results is
generated (either immediately or when next required). The first `n`
words are skipped (this may be used to set a specific word position).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This method will panic if `n >= N` where `N` is the buffer size (in
words).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#211-214)#### pub fn [word_offset](https://docs.rs#method.word_offset)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#211-214)

Get the number of words consumed since the start of the block

The result is in the range `0..N` where `N` is the buffer size (in
words).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#225-228)#### pub fn [remaining_results](https://docs.rs#method.remaining_results)(&self) -> &[[W]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.slice.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/block.rs.html#225-228)

#### pub fn [remaining_results](https://docs.rs#method.remaining_results)(&self) -> &[[W]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.slice.html)

Access the unused part of the results buffer

The length of the returned slice is guaranteed to be less than the
length of `<Self as Generator>::Output` (i.e. less than `N` where
`Output = [W; N]`).

This is a low-level interface intended for serialization. Results are not marked as consumed.

# UnwrapErr in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/struct.UnwrapErr.html

`pub struct UnwrapErr<R: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)>(pub R);## Expand description

Wrapper around [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) implementation which implements

[by panicking on potential errors.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
fn with_try_rng<R: TryRng>(mut rng: R) {
    // rng does not impl Rng:
    let _ = rng.try_next_u32(); // okay
    // let _ = rng.next_u32(); // error
    // An adapter borrowing rng:
    let _ = UnwrapErr(&mut rng).next_u32();
    // An adapter moving rng:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
fn call_with_unsized_try_rng<R: TryRng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) {
    // R is unsized, thus we must use &mut R:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
```

`0: R`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reborrow with a new lifetime

Rust allows references like `&T` or `&mut T` to be “reborrowed” through
coercion: essentially, the pointer is copied under a new, shorter, lifetime.
Until rfcs#1403 lands, reborrows on user types require a method call.

# TryRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.TryRng.html

```
pub trait TryRng {
    type
```
[Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error): [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html);
    // Required methods
    fn [try_next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u32)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u64)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
(`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
of [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
to avoid storing a partially used word or block.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#quality-and-length)Quality and length

Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).

Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a uniform-ranged distribution).

Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
but is a requirement of [ TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html).

In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.

For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality).

[§](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)Reproducibility

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes). See also

[The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Often, usage of the infallible trait [ Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) or its extension trait

[is preferred to direct usage of](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``TryRng`.
Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with `type Error = `[Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html))
already implement [; in other cases](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[may be used to obtain an implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)

`UnwrapErr`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-tryrng)Implementing `TryRng`

Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [ Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html); in this case
trait

`Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
error.Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
Module [ crate::utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html) provides utilities to help implement other methods.

Byte sources may implement [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)
natively.
Module

[provides utilities to help implement other methods.](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)

`crate::utils`Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
should make use of the [ crate::block](https://docs.rs/block/index.html) module.

With regards to other traits:

- **Do not**implement- `Default`
- **Do**implement- `SeedableRng`- [Reproducibility](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)above.
- Implement `Clone`
- **Do not**implement- `Copy`
- Implement `Debug`
- `Eq`- `PartialEq`

# SeedableRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/latest/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html

`pub trait SeedableRng: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    type [Seed](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Seed): [Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html) + [Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) + [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]> + [AsMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsMut.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]>;
