# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.10/

## Expand description

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of [PCG generators](https://www.pcg-random.org/).
The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in
other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

[§](https://docs.rs#generators)Generators

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`- `Lcg64Xsh32`- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`- `Lcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`- `Mcg128Xsl64`- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

These generators are all deterministic and portable (see [Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html)
in the book), with testing against reference vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#seeding-construction)Seeding (construction)

Generators implement the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/seedable_rng/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait. All methods are suitable for
seeding. Some suggestions:

- To automatically seed with a unique seed, use `SeedableRng::from_rng``rand::rng()`
- Seed **from an integer**via`seed_from_u64`. This uses a hash function internally to yield a (typically) good seed from any input.`let rng = Pcg64Mcg::seed_from_u64(1);`

See also [Seeding RNGs](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-seeding.html) in the book.

[§](https://docs.rs#generation)Generation

Generators implement [ Rng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.Rng.html), whose methods may be used directly to
generate unbounded integer or byte values.

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, Rng};
use rand_pcg::Pcg64Mcg;
let mut rng = Pcg64Mcg::seed_from_u64(0);
let x = rng.next_u64();
assert_eq!(x, 0x5603f242407deca2);
```
It is often more convenient to use the [ rand::Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.rng.html) trait, which provides
further functionality. See also the

[Random Values](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-values.html)chapter in the book.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A PCG random number generator (XSH RR 64/32 (LCG) variant).
- [Lcg128](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg128CmDxsm64.html)- CmDxsm64
- A PCG random number generator (CM DXSM 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- [Lcg128](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg128Xsl64.html)- Xsl64
- A PCG random number generator (XSL RR 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- [Mcg128](https://docs.rs/struct.Mcg128Xsl64.html)- Xsl64

# rayon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rayon/^1.7/

## Expand description

Rayon is a data-parallelism library that makes it easy to convert sequential computations into parallel.

It is lightweight and convenient for introducing parallelism into existing code. It guarantees data-race free executions and takes advantage of parallelism when sensible, based on work-load at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-use-rayon)How to use Rayon

There are two ways to use Rayon:

- **High-level parallel constructs**are the simplest way to use Rayon and also typically the most efficient.- [Parallel iterators](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)make it easy to convert a sequential iterator to execute in parallel.- The `ParallelIterator`
- The `IndexedParallelIterator`

- The
- The `par_sort``&mut [T]`slices (or vectors) in parallel.
- `par_extend`

- **Custom tasks**let you divide your work into parallel tasks yourself.- `join`
- `scope`
- `ThreadPoolBuilder`

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-and-the-rayon-prelude)Basic usage and the Rayon prelude

First, you will need to add `rayon` to your `Cargo.toml`.

Next, to use parallel iterators or the other high-level methods,
you need to import several traits. Those traits are bundled into
the module [ rayon::prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html). It is recommended that you import
all of these traits at once by adding

`use rayon::prelude::*` at
the top of each module that uses Rayon methods.These traits give you access to the `par_iter` method which provides
parallel implementations of many iterative functions such as [ map](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.map),

[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.for_each)

`for_each`[,](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.filter)

`filter`[, and](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#method.fold)

`fold`[more](https://docs.rs/iter/trait.ParallelIterator.html#provided-methods).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-layout)Crate Layout

Rayon extends many of the types found in the standard library with
parallel iterator implementations. The modules in the `rayon`
crate mirror [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) itself: so, e.g., the

`option` module in
Rayon contains parallel iterators for the `Option` type, which is
found in [the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/index.html). Similarly, the

`option` module of `std``collections` module in Rayon offers parallel iterator types for
[the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/index.html). You will rarely need to access these submodules unless you need to name iterator types explicitly.

`collections` from `std`[§](https://docs.rs#targets-without-threading)Targets without threading

Rayon has limited support for targets without `std` threading implementations.
See the [ rayon_core](https://docs.rs/rayon-core/1.13.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rayon_core/index.html) documentation for more information about its global fallback.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-questions)Other questions?

See [the Rayon FAQ](https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/main/FAQ.md).

See `scope()`
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeFifo.html)- Fifo

Those spawned from the same thread are prioritized in relative FIFO order.
See `scope_fifo()`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [broadcast](https://docs.rs/fn.broadcast.html)
- Executes `op`within every thread in the current thread pool. If this is called from a non-Rayon thread, it will execute in the global thread pool. Any attempts to use`join`,`scope`, or parallel iterators will then operate within that thread pool. When the call has completed on each thread, returns a vector containing all of their return values.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the number of threads in the current registry. If this code is executing within a Rayon thread pool, then this will be the number of threads for the thread pool of the current thread. Otherwise, it will be the number of threads for the global thread pool.
- [current_](https://docs.rs/fn.current_thread_index.html)- thread_ - index
- If called from a Rayon worker thread, returns the index of that
thread within its current pool; if not called from a Rayon thread,
returns `None`.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope.html)- place_ - scope
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [in_](https://docs.rs/fn.in_place_scope_fifo.html)- place_ - scope_ - fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [join](https://docs.rs/fn.join.html)
- Takes two closures and *potentially*runs them in parallel. It returns a pair of the results from those closures.
- [join_](https://docs.rs/fn.join_context.html)- context
- Identical to `join`, except that the closures have a parameter that provides context for the way the closure has been called, especially indicating whether they’re executing on a different thread than where`join_context`was called. This will occur if the second job is stolen by a different thread, or if`join_context`was called from outside the thread pool to begin with.
- [max_](https://docs.rs/fn.max_num_threads.html)- num_ - threads
- Returns the maximum number of threads that Rayon supports in a single thread pool.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [scope_](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)- fifo
- Creates a “fork-join” scope `s`with FIFO order, and invokes the closure with a reference to`s`. This closure can then spawn asynchronous tasks into`s`. Those tasks may run asynchronously with respect to the closure; they may themselves spawn additional tasks into`s`. When the closure returns, it will block until all tasks that have been spawned into`s`complete.
- [spawn](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn.html)
- Puts the task into the Rayon thread pool’s job queue in the “static”
or “global” scope. Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope.html)to create a scope.`scope()`function
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_broadcast.html)- broadcast
- Spawns an asynchronous task on every thread in this thread pool. This task
will run in the implicit, global scope, which means that it may outlast the
current stack frame – therefore, it cannot capture any references onto the
stack (you will likely need a `move`closure).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_fifo.html)- fifo
- Fires off a task into the Rayon thread pool in the “static” or
“global” scope.  Just like a standard thread, this task is not
tied to the current stack frame, and hence it cannot hold any
references other than those with `'static`lifetime. If you want to spawn a task that references stack data, use[the](https://docs.rs/fn.scope_fifo.html)to create a scope.`scope_fifo()`function
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_local.html)- local
- Cooperatively yields execution to local Rayon work.
- [yield_](https://docs.rs/fn.yield_now.html)- now
- Cooperatively yields execution to Rayon.

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0.140/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize JSON data to a Rust data structure.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- When serializing or deserializing JSON goes wrong.
- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- A map of String to serde_json::Value.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)- `std`
- Serialize a Rust data structure into JSON data.
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- The Value enum, a loosely typed way of representing any valid JSON value.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [json](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html)
- Construct a `serde_json::Value`from a JSON literal.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Deserializer.html)
- A structure that deserializes JSON into Rust values.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- This type represents all possible errors that can occur when serializing or deserializing JSON data.
- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- Represents a JSON key/value type.
- [Number](https://docs.rs/struct.Number.html)
- Represents a JSON number, whether integer or floating point.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)- `std`
- A structure for serializing Rust values into JSON.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDeserializer.html)- Deserializer
- Iterator that deserializes a stream into multiple JSON values.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html)
- Represents any valid JSON value.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)- reader - `std`
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from an I/O stream of JSON.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)- slice
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from bytes of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html)- str
- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from a string of JSON text.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value.html)- value
- Interpret a `serde_json::Value`as an instance of type`T`.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html)- string - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string_pretty.html)- string_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed String of JSON.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_value.html)- value
- Convert a `T`into`serde_json::Value`which is an enum that can represent any valid JSON data.
- [to_vec](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)- `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec_pretty.html)- vec_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as a pretty-printed JSON byte vector.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)- writer - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as JSON into the I/O stream.
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer_pretty.html)- writer_ - pretty - `std`
- Serialize the given data structure as pretty-printed JSON into the I/O stream.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Alias for a `Result`with the error type`serde_json::Error`.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/latest/target-redirect/rand/

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [distr](https://docs.rs/distr/index.html)
- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [RngReader](https://docs.rs/struct.RngReader.html)- `std`
- Adapter to support `std::io::Read``TryRng`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs
- [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html)
- Support filling a slice with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- Trait for infallible random number generators
- [RngExt](https://docs.rs/trait.RngExt.html)
- User-level interface for RNGs
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `TryRng`
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)
- Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill](https://docs.rs/fn.fill.html)- `thread_rng`
- Fill any type implementing `Fill`
- [make_](https://docs.rs/fn.make_rng.html)- rng - `sys_rng`
- Construct and seed an RNG
- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_bool.html)- bool - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability `p`of being true.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_iter.html)- iter - `thread_rng`
- Return an iterator over `random()`
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_range.html)- range - `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value in the given range using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_ratio.html)- ratio - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator`of being true.
- [rng](https://docs.rs/fn.rng.html)- `thread_rng`
- Access a fast, pre-initialized generator

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Wrapper around `TryRng``Rng`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html)
- The error type for errors that can never happen.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- Trait for infallible random number generators
- [RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html)- Deprecated
- DEPRECATED: stub trait to print a deprecation warning and aid discovering that `Rng`
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG)

of these traits.
Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

# rand_core::block - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/block/index.html

## Expand description

The [ Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html) trait and

`BlockRng`Trait [ Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html) may be implemented by block-generators; that is PRNGs
whose output is a

*block*of words, such as

`[u32; 16]`.The struct [ BlockRng](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html) wraps such a

[together with an output buffer and implements several methods (e.g.](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html)

`Generator`[) to assist in the implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html#method.next_word)

`BlockRng::next_word`[. Note that (unlike in earlier versions of](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)

`TryRng``rand_core`) [itself does not implement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html)

`BlockRng`[since in practice we found it was always beneficial to use a wrapper type over](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)

`TryRng`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html)

`BlockRng`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use core::convert::Infallible;
use rand_core::{Rng, SeedableRng, TryRng};
use rand_core::block::{Generator, BlockRng};
struct MyRngCore {
    // Generator state ...
}
impl Generator for MyRngCore {
    type Output = [u32; 8];
    fn generate(&mut self, output: &mut Self::Output) {
        // Write a new block to output...
    }
}
// Our RNG is a wrapper over BlockRng
pub struct MyRng(BlockRng<MyRngCore>);
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = [u8; 32];
    fn from_seed(seed: Self::Seed) -> Self {
        let core = MyRngCore {
            // ...
        };
        MyRng(BlockRng::new(core))
    }
}
impl TryRng for MyRng {
    type Error = Infallible;
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.next_word())
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.next_u64_from_u32())
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, bytes: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.fill_bytes(bytes))
    }
}
// And if applicable: impl TryCryptoRng for MyRng {}
let mut rng = MyRng::seed_from_u64(0);
println!("First value: {}", rng.next_u32());
```

# rand_core::utils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/utils/index.html

## Expand description

Utilties to aid trait implementations

[§](https://docs.rs#portability)Portability

For cross-platform reproducibility, Little-Endian order (least-significant
part first) has been chosen as the standard for inter-type conversion.
For example, [ next_u64_via_u32](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html) generates two

`u32` values `x, y`,
then outputs `(y << 32) | x`.Byte-swapping (like the std `to_le` functions) is only needed to convert
to/from byte sequences, and since its purpose is reproducibility,
non-reproducible sources (e.g. `OsRng`) need not bother with it.

Usually an implementation of [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) will implement one of the three
methods over its internal source. The following helpers are provided for
the remaining implementations.

`fn try_next_u32`:

- `self.next_u64() as u32`
- `(self.next_u64() >> 32) as u32`
- [next_word_via_fill](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)(self)

`fn try_next_u64`:

- [next_u64_via_u32](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html)(self)
- [next_word_via_fill](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)(self)

`fn try_fill_bytes`:

- [fill_bytes_via_next_word](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_bytes_via_next_word.html)(self, dest)

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng)Implementing `SeedableRng`

`SeedableRng`In many cases, [ SeedableRng::Seed](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#associatedtype.Seed) must be converted to

`[u32; _]` or
`[u64; _]`. [may be used for this.](https://docs.rs/fn.read_words.html)

`read_words`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

We demonstrate a simple multiplicative congruential generator (MCG), taken
from M.E. O’Neill’s blog post [Does It Beat the Minimal Standard?](https://www.pcg-random.org/posts/does-it-beat-the-minimal-standard.html).

```
use core::convert::Infallible;
use rand_core::{Rng, SeedableRng, TryRng, utils};
pub struct Mcg128(u128);
impl SeedableRng for Mcg128 {
    type Seed = [u8; 16];
    #[inline]
    fn from_seed(seed: Self::Seed) -> Self {
        // Always use little-endian byte order to ensure portable results
        Self(u128::from_le_bytes(seed))
    }
}
impl TryRng for Mcg128 {
    type Error = Infallible;
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
        Ok((self.next_u64() >> 32) as u32)
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Infallible> {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(0x0fc94e3bf4e9ab32866458cd56f5e605);
        Ok((self.0 >> 64) as u64)
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, dst: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
        utils::fill_bytes_via_next_word(dst, || self.try_next_u64())
    }
}
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Word](https://docs.rs/trait.Word.html)
- A marker trait for supported “word” types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_bytes_via_next_word.html)- bytes_ - via_ - next_ - word
- Fill `dst`with bytes using`next_word`
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html)- u64_ - via_ - u32
- Generate a `u64`using`next_u32`, little-endian order.
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)- word_ - via_ - fill
- Generate a `u32`or`u64`word using`fill_bytes`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_words.html)- words
- Reads an array of words from a byte slice

# UnwrapErr in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/struct.UnwrapErr.html

`pub struct UnwrapErr<R: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)>(pub R);## Expand description

Wrapper around [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) implementation which implements

[by panicking on potential errors.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
fn with_try_rng<R: TryRng>(mut rng: R) {
    // rng does not impl Rng:
    let _ = rng.try_next_u32(); // okay
    // let _ = rng.next_u32(); // error
    // An adapter borrowing rng:
    let _ = UnwrapErr(&mut rng).next_u32();
    // An adapter moving rng:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
fn call_with_unsized_try_rng<R: TryRng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) {
    // R is unsized, thus we must use &mut R:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
```

`0: R`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reborrow with a new lifetime

Rust allows references like `&T` or `&mut T` to be “reborrowed” through
coercion: essentially, the pointer is copied under a new, shorter, lifetime.
Until rfcs#1403 lands, reborrows on user types require a method call.

# TryRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/trait.TryRng.html

```
pub trait TryRng {
    type
```
[Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error): [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html);
    // Required methods
    fn [try_next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u32)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u64)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
(`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
of [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
to avoid storing a partially used word or block.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#quality-and-length)Quality and length

Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).

Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a uniform-ranged distribution).

Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
but is a requirement of [ TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html).

In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.

For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality).

[§](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)Reproducibility

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes). See also

[The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Often, usage of the infallible trait [ Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) or its extension trait

[is preferred to direct usage of](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``TryRng`.
Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with `type Error = `[Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html))
already implement [; in other cases](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[may be used to obtain an implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)

`UnwrapErr`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-tryrng)Implementing `TryRng`

Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [ Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html); in this case
trait

`Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
error.Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
Module [ crate::utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html) provides utilities to help implement other methods.

Byte sources may implement [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)
natively.
Module

[provides utilities to help implement other methods.](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)

`crate::utils`Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
should make use of the [ crate::block](https://docs.rs/block/index.html) module.

With regards to other traits:

- **Do not**implement- `Default`
- **Do**implement- `SeedableRng`- [Reproducibility](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)above.
- Implement `Clone`
- **Do not**implement- `Copy`
- Implement `Debug`
- `Eq`- `PartialEq`

# Rng in rand_core - Rust

Trait for infallible random number generators

`Rng` is a sub-trait of [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) for infallible generators.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

See [ TryRng#Requirements](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#Requirements) which also apply here.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand/) crate provides higher level functionality, for example
generation of floating-point values, uniform ranged sampling and shuffling
sequences. In particular,

[is an extension trait over](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``Rng`
providing many of the methods one might expect to be able to use on an RNG.[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-rng)Implementing `Rng`

`type Error = `[core::convert::Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html).## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand_core/lib.rs.html#62)#### fn [fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)])

Fill `dest` with random data.

This method should guarantee that `dest` is entirely filled
with new data, and may panic if this is impossible
(e.g. reading past the end of a file that is being used as the
source of randomness).

# TryCryptoRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/rand_core/trait.TryCryptoRng.html

`pub trait TryCryptoRng: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) { }## Expand description

A marker trait over [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) for securely unpredictable RNGs

This marker trait indicates that the implementing generator is intended, when correctly seeded and protected from side-channel attacks such as a leaking of state, to be a cryptographically secure generator. This trait is provided as a tool to aid review of cryptographic code, but does not by itself guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications.

Formally, a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
should satisfy an additional property over other generators: assuming that
the generator has been appropriately seeded and has unknown state, then
given the first *k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

An optional property of CSPRNGs is backtracking resistance: if the CSPRNG’s
state is revealed, it will not be computationally-feasible to reconstruct
prior output values. This property is not required by `CryptoRng`.

Implementors of `TryCryptoRng` should only implement [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) if a
default-constructed instance is itself a secure generator, for example

[which is a stateless interface.](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/struct.SysRng.html)

`getrandom::SysRng`

---

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

[98](https://docs.rs#98)
[99](https://docs.rs#99)/// Base trait for random number generators and random data sources
[100](https://docs.rs#100)///
[101](https://docs.rs#101)/// This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
[102](https://docs.rs#102)/// (`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
[103](https://docs.rs#103)/// There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
[104](https://docs.rs#104)/// requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// of [`try_fill_bytes`](Self::try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// to avoid storing a partially used word or block.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// # Requirements
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// ### Quality and length
[111](https://docs.rs#111)///
[112](https://docs.rs#112)/// Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// uniform-ranged distribution).
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// but is a requirement of [`TryCryptoRng`].
[125](https://docs.rs#125)///
[126](https://docs.rs#126)/// In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
[127](https://docs.rs#127)/// finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
[128](https://docs.rs#128)/// statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
[130](https://docs.rs#130)/// anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.
[131](https://docs.rs#131)///
[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality][0].
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// [0]: https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality
[135](https://docs.rs#135)///
[136](https://docs.rs#136)/// ### Reproducibility
[137](https://docs.rs#137)///
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// Algorithmic generators implementing [`SeedableRng`] should normally have
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// *portable, reproducible* output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values
[140](https://docs.rs#140)/// to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes).
[142](https://docs.rs#142)/// See also [The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility][1].
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// [1]: https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// # Usage
[147](https://docs.rs#147)///
[148](https://docs.rs#148)/// Often, usage of the infallible trait [`Rng`] or its extension trait
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// [`rand::RngExt`] is preferred to direct usage of `TryRng`.
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with <code>type Error = [Infallible][]</code>)
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// already implement [`Rng`]; in other cases [`UnwrapErr`] may be used to obtain
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// an implementation of [`Rng`].
[154](https://docs.rs#154)///
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// # Implementing `TryRng`
[156](https://docs.rs#156)///
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [`Infallible`]; in this case
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// trait `Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
[160](https://docs.rs#160)/// error.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)///
[162](https://docs.rs#162)/// Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)/// Module [`crate::utils`] provides utilities to help implement other methods.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)/// Byte sources may implement [`try_fill_bytes`](Self::try_fill_bytes)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)/// natively.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)/// Module [`crate::utils`] provides utilities to help implement other methods.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)///
[169](https://docs.rs#169)/// Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)/// should make use of the [`crate::block`] module.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// With regards to other traits:
[173](https://docs.rs#173)///
[174](https://docs.rs#174)/// - **Do not** implement [`Default`] for seedable pseudorandom generators,
[175](https://docs.rs#175)///   though the trait may be implemented for stateless interfaces and
[176](https://docs.rs#176)///   auto-seeding generators.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// - **Do** implement [`SeedableRng`] for seedable pseudorandom generators. See
[178](https://docs.rs#178)///   [Reproducibility](#reproducibility) above.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// - Implement [`Clone`] for non-cryptographic PRNGs but consider not doing so
[180](https://docs.rs#180)///   for cryptographic generators to avoid the risk of key-stream duplication.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)/// - **Do not** implement [`Copy`] since accidental copies may cause repeated
[182](https://docs.rs#182)///   values.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)/// - Implement [`Debug`](core::fmt::Debug), except that cryptographic PRNGs
[184](https://docs.rs#184)///   should use a custom implementation which avoids leaking internal state (or
[185](https://docs.rs#185)///   the subset of this derived from the key).
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// - [`Eq`] and [`PartialEq`] could be implemented, but are probably not useful.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///
[188](https://docs.rs#188)/// [`rand::RngExt`]: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html
[189](https://docs.rs#189)pub trait [TryRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/trait.TryRng.html) {

[194](https://docs.rs#194)

[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// A marker trait over [`TryRng`] for securely unpredictable RNGs
[226](https://docs.rs#226)///
[227](https://docs.rs#227)/// This marker trait indicates that the implementing generator is intended,
[228](https://docs.rs#228)/// when correctly seeded and protected from side-channel attacks such as a
[229](https://docs.rs#229)/// leaking of state, to be a cryptographically secure generator. This trait is
[230](https://docs.rs#230)/// provided as a tool to aid review of cryptographic code, but does not by
[231](https://docs.rs#231)/// itself guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)///
[233](https://docs.rs#233)/// Formally, a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)/// should satisfy an additional property over other generators: assuming that
[235](https://docs.rs#235)/// the generator has been appropriately seeded and has unknown state, then
[236](https://docs.rs#236)/// given the first *k* bits of an algorithm's output
[237](https://docs.rs#237)/// sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)///
[240](https://docs.rs#240)/// An optional property of CSPRNGs is backtracking resistance: if the CSPRNG's
[241](https://docs.rs#241)/// state is revealed, it will not be computationally-feasible to reconstruct
[242](https://docs.rs#242)/// prior output values. This property is not required by `CryptoRng`.
[243](https://docs.rs#243)///
[244](https://docs.rs#244)/// Implementors of `TryCryptoRng` should only implement [`Default`] if a
[245](https://docs.rs#245)/// default-constructed instance is itself a secure generator, for example
[246](https://docs.rs#246)/// [`getrandom::SysRng`] which is a stateless interface.
[247](https://docs.rs#247)///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)/// [`getrandom::SysRng`]: https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/struct.SysRng.html
[249](https://docs.rs#249)pub trait [TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/trait.TryCryptoRng.html): [TryRng](https://docs.rs#189-201) {}

# rand_core::utils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/utils/index.html

## Expand description

Utilties to aid trait implementations

[§](https://docs.rs#portability)Portability

For cross-platform reproducibility, Little-Endian order (least-significant
part first) has been chosen as the standard for inter-type conversion.
For example, [ next_u64_via_u32](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html) generates two

`u32` values `x, y`,
then outputs `(y << 32) | x`.Byte-swapping (like the std `to_le` functions) is only needed to convert
to/from byte sequences, and since its purpose is reproducibility,
non-reproducible sources (e.g. `OsRng`) need not bother with it.

Usually an implementation of [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) will implement one of the three
methods over its internal source. The following helpers are provided for
the remaining implementations.

`fn try_next_u32`:

- `self.next_u64() as u32`
- `(self.next_u64() >> 32) as u32`
- [next_word_via_fill](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)(self)

`fn try_next_u64`:

- [next_u64_via_u32](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html)(self)
- [next_word_via_fill](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)(self)

`fn try_fill_bytes`:

- [fill_bytes_via_next_word](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_bytes_via_next_word.html)(self, dest)

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng)Implementing `SeedableRng`

`SeedableRng`In many cases, [ SeedableRng::Seed](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#associatedtype.Seed) must be converted to

`[u32; _]` or
`[u64; _]`. [may be used for this.](https://docs.rs/fn.read_words.html)

`read_words`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

We demonstrate a simple multiplicative congruential generator (MCG), taken
from M.E. O’Neill’s blog post [Does It Beat the Minimal Standard?](https://www.pcg-random.org/posts/does-it-beat-the-minimal-standard.html).

```
use core::convert::Infallible;
use rand_core::{Rng, SeedableRng, TryRng, utils};
pub struct Mcg128(u128);
impl SeedableRng for Mcg128 {
    type Seed = [u8; 16];
    #[inline]
    fn from_seed(seed: Self::Seed) -> Self {
        // Always use little-endian byte order to ensure portable results
        Self(u128::from_le_bytes(seed))
    }
}
impl TryRng for Mcg128 {
    type Error = Infallible;
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
        Ok((self.next_u64() >> 32) as u32)
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Infallible> {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(0x0fc94e3bf4e9ab32866458cd56f5e605);
        Ok((self.0 >> 64) as u64)
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, dst: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
        utils::fill_bytes_via_next_word(dst, || self.try_next_u64())
    }
}
```
## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Word](https://docs.rs/trait.Word.html)
- A marker trait for supported “word” types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_bytes_via_next_word.html)- bytes_ - via_ - next_ - word
- Fill `dst`with bytes using`next_word`
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html)- u64_ - via_ - u32
- Generate a `u64`using`next_u32`, little-endian order.
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)- word_ - via_ - fill
- Generate a `u32`or`u64`word using`fill_bytes`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_words.html)- words
- Reads an array of words from a byte slice

# UnwrapErr in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/struct.UnwrapErr.html

`pub struct UnwrapErr<R: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)>(pub R);## Expand description

Wrapper around [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) implementation which implements

[by panicking on potential errors.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
fn with_try_rng<R: TryRng>(mut rng: R) {
    // rng does not impl Rng:
    let _ = rng.try_next_u32(); // okay
    // let _ = rng.next_u32(); // error
    // An adapter borrowing rng:
    let _ = UnwrapErr(&mut rng).next_u32();
    // An adapter moving rng:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
fn call_with_unsized_try_rng<R: TryRng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) {
    // R is unsized, thus we must use &mut R:
    let mut rng = UnwrapErr(rng);
    let _ = rng.next_u32();
}
```

`0: R`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Reborrow with a new lifetime

Rust allows references like `&T` or `&mut T` to be “reborrowed” through
coercion: essentially, the pointer is copied under a new, shorter, lifetime.
Until rfcs#1403 lands, reborrows on user types require a method call.

# Infallible in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/enum.Infallible.html

`pub enum Infallible {}`## Expand description

The error type for errors that can never happen.

Since this enum has no variant, a value of this type can never actually exist.
This can be useful for generic APIs that use [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html) and parameterize the error type,
to indicate that the result is always

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)

`Ok`For example, the [ TryFrom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html) trait (conversion that returns a

[) has a blanket implementation for all types where a reverse](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[implementation exists.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T, U> TryFrom<U> for T where U: Into<T> {
    type Error = Infallible;
    fn try_from(value: U) -> Result<Self, Infallible> {
        Ok(U::into(value))  // Never returns `Err`
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#future-compatibility)Future compatibility

This enum has the same role as [the  ! “never” type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.never.html),
which is unstable in this version of Rust.
When

`!` is stabilized, we plan to make `Infallible` a type alias to it:… and eventually deprecate `Infallible`.

However there is one case where `!` syntax can be used
before `!` is stabilized as a full-fledged type: in the position of a function’s return type.
Specifically, it is possible to have implementations for two different function pointer types:

```
trait MyTrait {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> ! {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> std::convert::Infallible {}
```
With `Infallible` being an enum, this code is valid.
However when `Infallible` becomes an alias for the never type,
the two `impl`s will start to overlap
and therefore will be disallowed by the language’s trait coherence rules.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# TryCryptoRng in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.TryCryptoRng.html

`pub trait TryCryptoRng: `[TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) { }## Expand description

A marker trait over [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) for securely unpredictable RNGs

This marker trait indicates that the implementing generator is intended, when correctly seeded and protected from side-channel attacks such as a leaking of state, to be a cryptographically secure generator. This trait is provided as a tool to aid review of cryptographic code, but does not by itself guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications.

Formally, a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
should satisfy an additional property over other generators: assuming that
the generator has been appropriately seeded and has unknown state, then
given the first *k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

An optional property of CSPRNGs is backtracking resistance: if the CSPRNG’s
state is revealed, it will not be computationally-feasible to reconstruct
prior output values. This property is not required by `CryptoRng`.

Implementors of `TryCryptoRng` should only implement [ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) if a
default-constructed instance is itself a secure generator, for example

[which is a stateless interface.](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/struct.SysRng.html)

`getrandom::SysRng`

---

# rand_core::block - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/rand_core/block/index.html

## Expand description

The [ Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html) trait and

`BlockRng`Trait [ Generator](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html) may be implemented by block-generators; that is PRNGs
whose output is a

*block*of words, such as

`[u32; 16]`.The struct [ BlockRng](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html) wraps such a

[together with an output buffer and implements several methods (e.g.](https://docs.rs/trait.Generator.html)

`Generator`[) to assist in the implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html#method.next_word)

`BlockRng::next_word`[. Note that (unlike in earlier versions of](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)

`TryRng``rand_core`) [itself does not implement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html)

`BlockRng`[since in practice we found it was always beneficial to use a wrapper type over](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)

`TryRng`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.BlockRng.html)

`BlockRng`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use core::convert::Infallible;
use rand_core::{Rng, SeedableRng, TryRng};
use rand_core::block::{Generator, BlockRng};
struct MyRngCore {
    // Generator state ...
}
impl Generator for MyRngCore {
    type Output = [u32; 8];
    fn generate(&mut self, output: &mut Self::Output) {
        // Write a new block to output...
    }
}
// Our RNG is a wrapper over BlockRng
pub struct MyRng(BlockRng<MyRngCore>);
impl SeedableRng for MyRng {
    type Seed = [u8; 32];
    fn from_seed(seed: Self::Seed) -> Self {
        let core = MyRngCore {
            // ...
        };
        MyRng(BlockRng::new(core))
    }
}
impl TryRng for MyRng {
    type Error = Infallible;
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.next_word())
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.next_u64_from_u32())
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, bytes: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
        Ok(self.0.fill_bytes(bytes))
    }
}
// And if applicable: impl TryCryptoRng for MyRng {}
let mut rng = MyRng::seed_from_u64(0);
println!("First value: {}", rng.next_u32());
```

A random (block) generator

The output type.

For use with `rand_core::block``[u32; _]` or `[u64; _]`.

Generate a new block of `output`.

This must fill `output` with random data.

Destruct the output buffer

# rand_core::utils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/rand_core/utils/index.html

## Expand description

Utilties to aid trait implementations

[§](https://docs.rs#portability)Portability

For cross-platform reproducibility, Little-Endian order (least-significant
part first) has been chosen as the standard for inter-type conversion.
For example, [ next_u64_via_u32](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html) generates two

`u32` values `x, y`,
then outputs `(y << 32) | x`.Byte-swapping (like the std `to_le` functions) is only needed to convert
to/from byte sequences, and since its purpose is reproducibility,
non-reproducible sources (e.g. `OsRng`) need not bother with it.

Usually an implementation of [ TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html) will implement one of the three
methods over its internal source. The following helpers are provided for
the remaining implementations.

`fn try_next_u32`:

- `self.next_u64() as u32`
- `(self.next_u64() >> 32) as u32`
- [next_word_via_fill](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)(self)

`fn try_next_u64`:

- [next_u64_via_u32](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html)(self)
- [next_word_via_fill](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)(self)

`fn try_fill_bytes`:

- [fill_bytes_via_next_word](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_bytes_via_next_word.html)(self, dest)

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-seedablerng)Implementing `SeedableRng`

`SeedableRng`In many cases, [ SeedableRng::Seed](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#associatedtype.Seed) must be converted to

`[u32; _]` or
`[u64; _]`. [may be used for this.](https://docs.rs/fn.read_words.html)

`read_words`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

We demonstrate a simple multiplicative congruential generator (MCG), taken
from M.E. O’Neill’s blog post [Does It Beat the Minimal Standard?](https://www.pcg-random.org/posts/does-it-beat-the-minimal-standard.html).

```
use core::convert::Infallible;
use rand_core::{Rng, SeedableRng, TryRng, utils};
pub struct Mcg128(u128);
impl SeedableRng for Mcg128 {
    type Seed = [u8; 16];
    #[inline]
    fn from_seed(seed: Self::Seed) -> Self {
        // Always use little-endian byte order to ensure portable results
        Self(u128::from_le_bytes(seed))
    }
}
impl TryRng for Mcg128 {
    type Error = Infallible;
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u32(&mut self) -> Result<u32, Infallible> {
        Ok((self.next_u64() >> 32) as u32)
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_next_u64(&mut self) -> Result<u64, Infallible> {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_mul(0x0fc94e3bf4e9ab32866458cd56f5e605);
        Ok((self.0 >> 64) as u64)
    }
    #[inline]
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, dst: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Infallible> {
        utils::fill_bytes_via_next_word(dst, || self.try_next_u64())
    }
}
```

- A marker trait for supported “word” types.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_bytes_via_next_word.html)- bytes_ - via_ - next_ - word
- Fill `dst`with bytes using`next_word`
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_u64_via_u32.html)- u64_ - via_ - u32
- Generate a `u64`using`next_u32`, little-endian order.
- [next_](https://docs.rs/fn.next_word_via_fill.html)- word_ - via_ - fill
- Generate a `u32`or`u64`word using`fill_bytes`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_words.html)- words
- Reads an array of words from a byte slice

pub trait TryRng {
    type
```
[Error](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Error): [Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html);
    // Required methods
    fn [try_next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u32)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_next_u64)(&mut self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u64.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
[try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)(&mut self, dst: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#associatedtype.Error)>;
}## Expand description

Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

This trait provides a base interface designed to support efficient usage of
(`u32`, `u64`) word generators, block generators and random data sources.
There is no required relationship between the output of each method or any
requirement to use all generated random bits; for example an implementation
of [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) may discard some generated bytes
to avoid storing a partially used word or block.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

[§](https://docs.rs#quality-and-length)Quality and length

Implementions should produce bits uniformly: each output value should be equally likely, without observable patterns in successive outputs or between the output streams of multiple instances of an implementation using different seeds or streams (where supported by the implementation).

Pathological implementations (e.g. constant or counting generators which rarely change some bits) may cause issues in consumers of random data, for example dead-locks in rejection samplers and obviously non-random output (e.g. a counting generator may result in apparently-constant output from a uniform-ranged distribution).

Cryptographically unpredictable output is not a requirement of this trait,
but is a requirement of [ TryCryptoRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html).

In practice, most implementations are pseudo-random number generators with a
finite *period* or *cycle length*, and (among non-cryptographic PRNGs)
statistical anomalies may appear long before a cycle occurs. An
implementation should ensure its period is sufficiently long that no
anomalies are likely to appear in usage and/or document its limitations.

For more on PRNG quality and period, see [The Rust Rand Book: Quality](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#quality).

[§](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)Reproducibility

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes). See also

[The Rust Rand Book: Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Often, usage of the infallible trait [ Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html) or its extension trait

[is preferred to direct usage of](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html)

`rand::RngExt``TryRng`.
Many implementations of `TryRng` (those with `type Error = `[Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html))
already implement [; in other cases](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[may be used to obtain an implementation of](https://docs.rs/struct.UnwrapErr.html)

`UnwrapErr`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-tryrng)Implementing `TryRng`

Most algorithmic generators (i.e. pseudo-random number generators or PRNGs)
never fail; in this case type `Error` should be [ Infallible](https://docs.rs/enum.Infallible.html); in this case
trait

`Rng` is implemented automatically. Cycling is not considered an
error.Small PRNGs often yield either `u32` or `u64` natively.
Module [ crate::utils](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html) provides utilities to help implement other methods.

Byte sources may implement [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)
natively.
Module

[provides utilities to help implement other methods.](https://docs.rs/utils/index.html)

`crate::utils`Block generators (which produce `[u32; N]` or `[u64; N]` for some fixed `N`)
should make use of the [ crate::block](https://docs.rs/block/index.html) module.

With regards to other traits:

- **Do not**implement- `Default`
- **Do**implement- `SeedableRng`- [Reproducibility](https://docs.rs#reproducibility)above.
- Implement `Clone`
- **Do not**implement- `Copy`
- Implement `Debug`
- `Eq`- `PartialEq`

# Infallible in rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/rand_core/enum.Infallible.html

`pub enum Infallible {}`## Expand description

The error type for errors that can never happen.

Since this enum has no variant, a value of this type can never actually exist.
This can be useful for generic APIs that use [ Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html) and parameterize the error type,
to indicate that the result is always

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok)

`Ok`For example, the [ TryFrom](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.TryFrom.html) trait (conversion that returns a

[) has a blanket implementation for all types where a reverse](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[implementation exists.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)

`Into`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl<T, U> TryFrom<U> for T where U: Into<T> {
    type Error = Infallible;
    fn try_from(value: U) -> Result<Self, Infallible> {
        Ok(U::into(value))  // Never returns `Err`
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#future-compatibility)Future compatibility

This enum has the same role as [the  ! “never” type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.never.html),
which is unstable in this version of Rust.
When

`!` is stabilized, we plan to make `Infallible` a type alias to it:… and eventually deprecate `Infallible`.

However there is one case where `!` syntax can be used
before `!` is stabilized as a full-fledged type: in the position of a function’s return type.
Specifically, it is possible to have implementations for two different function pointer types:

```
trait MyTrait {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> ! {}
impl MyTrait for fn() -> std::convert::Infallible {}
```
With `Infallible` being an enum, this code is valid.
However when `Infallible` becomes an alias for the never type,
the two `impl`s will start to overlap
and therefore will be disallowed by the language’s trait coherence rules.

# rand_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand_core/0.10.1/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/rand_core/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rand_core-core-random-number-generation-traits)rand_core: core random number generation traits

This crate provides a collection of traits used by implementations of Random Number Generation (RNG) algorithms. Additionally, it includes helper utilities that assist with the implementation of these traits.

Note that the traits focus solely on the core RNG functionality. Most users should prefer
the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate, which offers more advanced RNG capabilities built on these core traits,
such as sampling from restricted ranges, generating floating-point numbers, list permutations,
and more.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

The crate is licensed under either of:

at your option.

[25](https://docs.rs#25)/// Trait for infallible random number generators
[26](https://docs.rs#26)///
[27](https://docs.rs#27)/// `Rng` is a sub-trait of [`TryRng`] for infallible generators.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)///
[29](https://docs.rs#29)/// # Requirements
[30](https://docs.rs#30)///
[31](https://docs.rs#31)/// See [`TryRng`#Requirements] which also apply here.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)///
[33](https://docs.rs#33)/// # Usage
[34](https://docs.rs#34)///
[35](https://docs.rs#35)/// The [`rand`] crate provides higher level functionality, for example
[36](https://docs.rs#36)/// generation of floating-point values, uniform ranged sampling and shuffling
[37](https://docs.rs#37)/// sequences. In particular, [`rand::RngExt`] is an extension trait over `Rng`
[38](https://docs.rs#38)/// providing many of the methods one might expect to be able to use on an RNG.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)///
[40](https://docs.rs#40)/// # Implementing `Rng`
[41](https://docs.rs#41)///
[42](https://docs.rs#42)/// Implement [`TryRng`] with <code>type Error = [core::convert::Infallible][]</code>.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)///
[44](https://docs.rs#44)/// [`rand`]: https://docs.rs/rand/
[45](https://docs.rs#45)/// [`rand::RngExt`]: https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/trait.RngExt.html
[46](https://docs.rs#46)/// [`fill_bytes`]: Rng::fill_bytes
